s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Live, Die
s.d: the process of dying
s.c: In a number of languages clear distinctions are made in the use of terms for dying on the basis of the manner or circumstances of death. For example, one term may refer to death primarily as the result of old age, while another term may refer to death caused by sickness, and still other terms may be used for death caused by violence. Careful distinctions must be used in determining the choice of terms based on particular contexts.|This first clause of ⟦2 Corinthians 4:10|2 Corinthians 4:10⟧ is highly elliptical, for it evidently refers to the fact that Paul was constantly in danger of dying in the same manner in which Jesus died, that is to say, by violence. One may render ⟦2 Corinthians 4:10|2 Corinthians 4:10⟧ as ‘at all times we live in the constant threat of being killed as Jesus was.’

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Birth, Procreation
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:νέκρωσις<SDBG:νέκρωσις:000000>}[a] ‘death,’ {D:23.99}) the state of not being able to bear children as the result of having passed through menopause

s.dp: Festivals
s.d: a festivity associated with the appearance of the new moon

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: pertaining to having been in existence for only a short time

s.dp: Nature, Class, Example › New, Old [primarily non-temporal]
s.d: pertaining to that which is new or recent and hence superior to that which is old{N:001}

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: pertaining to a living being who is relatively young, often the younger of two objects

s.dp: Time › Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
s.d: a period of time when one is young{N:001}

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Religious
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of νεόφυτος ‘newly planted,’ not occurring in the NT) an individual who has recently become a member of a religious group
s.c: A ‘recent convert’ may be rendered as ‘one who has only recently begun to believe in Christ’ or ‘one who has just begun to trust Christ.’

s.dp: Communication › Non-Verbal Communication
s.d: to signal to someone by means of part of the body, especially by means of the head or hands{N:001}
s.g: to gesture; to motion; to nod; to beckon
s.c: In a number of languages it is necessary to be quite specific with regard to types of gestures or motions of the head or hands and arms. For example, in ⟦John 13:24|John 13:24⟧ there is an obvious question involved, and this may require in some languages a particular signal by means of the hands or face. The same would be true in the case of ⟦Luke 1:62|Luke 1:62⟧. In ⟦Luke 1:22|Luke 1:22⟧ the gesture would have to be something which would explain or indicate Zechariah’s inability to speak, while in ⟦Luke 5:7|Luke 5:7⟧ quite another gesture would no doubt be called for, since the persons involved were at quite a distance from one another.

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Atmospheric Objects
s.d: visible mass of particles of water in the sky; varies in color from white to dark grey; source of rain
s.c: In many languages it would be difficult to speak of ‘a cloud coming up in the west,’ for this would seem to imply that a cloud was actually rising from below the earth. In some languages it is better to speak of ‘a cloud getting larger’ or, in the specific context of ⟦Luke 12:54|Luke 12:54⟧, one may translate ‘when you see a cloud coming to you from the west.’

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Atmospheric Objects
s.d: a cloud-like mass of moisture close to the earth's surface
s.c: In the NT ὁμίχλη is used only figuratively: οὗτοί εἰσιν πηγαὶ ἄνυδροι καὶ ὁμίχλαι ὑπὸ λαίλαπος ἐλαυνόμεναι ‘these men are dried up springs or mists blown along by a storm’ ⟦2 Peter 2:17|2 Peter 2:17⟧. The metaphorical usage in ⟦2 Peter 2:17|2 Peter 2:17⟧ must be marked in a number of languages as a simile, for example, ‘these men are like springs that have dried up and are like mists which the storm blows along.’

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a son of Jacob and ancestor of an Israelite tribe

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: the territory of the tribe of Naphtali

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › General
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of νέφος ‘cloud,’ not occurring in the NT) a large crowd of people
s.c: In ⟦Hebrews 12:1|Hebrews 12:1⟧ a possible supplementary component of ‘heavenly’ is applicable, since the reference is to the heroes of faith mentioned in chapter 11. In general one cannot preserve the figure of speech, nor even a term meaning ‘crowd,’ since the persons in chapter 11 did not form a crowd historically. A more common equivalent of ‘large crowd of witnesses’ is ‘many, many witnesses.’

s.dp: Psychological Faculties
s.d: (figurative extension of meaning of νεφρός ‘kidney,’ not occurring in its literal meaning in the NT) the psychological faculty of desire, intent, and feeling{N:001}
s.c: Though some persons have attempted to distinguish between σπλάγχνον, κοιλία, and νεφρός, it is extremely doubtful whether this is really possible or practical. The semantic focus in the use of these terms is clearly the deeper and more intimate feelings and emotions. In some languages one can use a term which literally means ‘belly’ or ‘bowels,’ but more often than not, these emotions are associated with some particular organ of the body such as heart, spleen, liver, etc. Rather, however, than attempting to employ a figurative expression which may or may not be fully equivalent, it is often preferable to refer to the emotional content by using terms such as ‘feelings,’ ‘intents,’ ‘desires,’ or ‘compassion,’ depending upon the context.

s.dp: Religious Activities › Roles and Functions
s.d: one who had responsibility to tend to and to guard a temple
s.c: In ⟦Acts 19:35|Acts 19:35⟧ νεωκόρος is used in a somewhat figurative sense, since it is the city of Ephesus itself which is regarded as being the keeper of the temple.

s.dp: Time › Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
s.d: pertaining to the period of time when one is an adolescent{N:001}

s.dp: Relations › Basis
s.d: a marker of the basis for an oath or strong declaration
s.g: on the basis of; by virtue of
s.c: Because of the elliptical nature of this expression in ⟦1 Corinthians 15:31|1 Corinthians 15:31⟧, the semantic implications of νή are often omitted, or the implication of νή is introduced by employing an overt declaration, as in Today’s English Version, “The pride I have in you, in our life in union with Christ Jesus our Lord, makes me declare this.”

s.dp: Activities Involving Cloth
s.d: to make yarn by twisting fibers together as one of the steps in making cloth

s.dp: People › Children
s.d: to be or to become like a child
s.g: to be as a child; to be childlike

s.dp: People › Children
s.d: a small child above the age of a helpless infant but probably not more than three or four years of age
s.c: In ⟦Romans 2:20|Romans 2:20⟧ the Greek expression διδάσκαλον νηπίων, literally ‘teacher of little children,’ may be better understood in a sense of ‘teacher of the ignorant’ or ‘teacher of the unlearned.’

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a person greeted in {S:04501601500010}

s.d: a person in the genealogy of Jesus

Geographical Objects and Features › Land in Contrast With the Sea
s.d: an area of land completely surrounded by water
s.c: In some languages an island can only be designated by a description, for example, ‘a small country in the sea’ or ‘some land surrounded by water.’

s.d: to go without food for a set time as a religious duty

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.d: the state of being very hungry, presumably for a considerable period of time and as the result of necessity rather than choice (compare {L:νηστεία<SDBG:νηστεία:000000>}[a] ‘fasting,’ {D:53.65})
s.g: to be quite hungry; considerable hunger; lack of food
s.c: Terms referring to hunger often distinguish varying degrees of hunger and whether the hunger is by necessity or by choice.

s.dp: Festivals
s.d: a Jewish festival celebrating the forgiveness of sins on the day of atonement{N:001}
s.g: festival of the atonement; day to commemorate the atonement of sin
s.c: The Day of Atonement in the Jewish calendar occurs in the fall, a time which is particularly dangerous to small ships in the Mediterranean. In biblical times, small merchant ships normally stayed in a harbor over the winter months.

s.dp: Religious Activities › Fasting
s.d: to go without food for a set time as a religious duty

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.d: the state of being very hungry, presumably for a considerable period of time and as the result of necessity rather than choice (compare {L:νηστεία<SDBG:νηστεία:000000>}[a] ‘fasting,’ {D:53.65})
s.g: to be quite hungry; considerable hunger; lack of food
s.c: Terms referring to hunger often distinguish varying degrees of hunger and whether the hunger is by necessity or by choice.

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Self-Control, Lack of Self-Control
s.d: (derivative of {L:νήφω<SDBG:νήφω:000001>}[b] ‘to be restrained,’ {D:88.86}) pertaining to behaving in a sober, restrained manner
s.c: In a number of languages νηφάλιος may be idiomatically rendered as ‘one who holds himself in’ or ‘one who always has a halter on himself.’

s.dp: Think › To Think, Thought
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of νήφω ‘to be sober, to not be drunk,’ probably not occurring in the NT; see {D:88.86}) to be in control of one’s thought processes and thus not be in danger of irrational thinking
s.g: to be sober-minded; to be well composed in mind
s.c: It is also possible to understand νήφω in ⟦1 Thessalonians 5:6|1 Thessalonians 5:6⟧ as meaning ‘self-control,’ as a characteristic of moral behavior (see LN 88.86).

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Self-Control, Lack of Self-Control
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of νήφω ‘to be sober,’ in the sense of ‘not being drunk,’ probably not occurring in the NT) to behave with restraint and moderation, thus not permitting excess
s.g: to be self-controlled; to be restrained; to be moderate in one’s behavior; to be sober
s.c: It is possible that in ⟦1 Thessalonians 5:8|1 Thessalonians 5:8⟧ νήφω means lack of drunkenness, but most scholars interpret the use of νήφω in the NT as applying to a broader range of soberness or sobriety, namely, restraint and moderation which avoids excess in passion, rashness, or confusion. For another interpretation of νήφω in ⟦1 Thessalonians 5:8|1 Thessalonians 5:8⟧, as well as in ⟦1 Thessalonians 5:6|1 Thessalonians 5:6⟧, see LN 30.25.

s.d: to win a victory over
s.g: to be victorious over; to be a victor; to conquer; victory
s.c: In ⟦1 John 5:4|1 John 5:4⟧ ‘the world’ must be understood in terms of the value system of the world. In a number of languages the closest equivalent of ‘to be victorious over’ is ‘to defeat.’

s.dp: Hostility, Strife › Conquer
s.d: to win a victory over
s.g: to be victorious over; to be a victor; to conquer; victory

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: one of the seven helpers in the church in Jerusalem

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a city on the west coast of Greece

s.dp: Hostility, Strife › Conquer
s.d: to win a victory over
s.g: to be victorious over; to be a victor; to conquer; victory

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: (derivative of Νινευή ‘Nineveh,’ not occurring in the NT) a person who lives in or is a native of Nineveh

s.dp: Artifacts › Containers
s.d: a large bowl, normally made of clay, used for washing of hands, face, and feet

s.dp: Activities Involving Liquids or Masses › Use of Liquids
s.d: to wash a part of a body, usually the hands or feet

s.dp: Association › Show Hospitality
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to wash the feet, derived from the practice of washing the feet of any guest entering the home) to show sincere and gracious hospitality to someone
s.c: It is also possible that the idiom πόδας νίπτω means ‘to perform humble duties on behalf of someone’ (see LN 88.58).

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Humility
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to wash the feet) to show humility by doing humble tasks
s.g: to act humbly; to behave in a humble manner
s.c: For another interpretation of πόδας νίπτω in ⟦1 Timothy 5:10|1 Timothy 5:10⟧, see LN 34.59.

s.dp: Understand
s.d: to comprehend something on the basis of careful thought and consideration
s.g: to perceive; to gain insight into; to understand; to comprehend

s.dp: Think › To Think, Thought
s.d: to think over a matter with care
s.g: to think about carefully; to consider well

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Have an Opinion, Hold a View
s.d: to be able to form some idea about
s.g: to be able to form an idea; to imagine
s.c: It is also possible to understand νοέω in ⟦Ephesians 3:20|Ephesians 3:20⟧ as meaning merely ‘to hold a particular view’ (compare LN 31.1), and therefore one may translate ‘far beyond what we think to be the case.’

s.dp: Psychological Faculties
s.d: the psychological faculty of understanding, reasoning, thinking, and deciding
s.c: In some languages there is no noun such as English mind, and therefore one must use a verb expression meaning ‘to think,’ ‘to reason,’ or ‘to understand,’ depending upon the particular context. In some languages the closest equivalent of ‘mind’ may be a figurative extension of a term meaning ‘head,’ but more often than not, thinking is regarded as being in some other part of the body, for example, ‘heart’ or ‘liver.’

s.dp: Think › To Think, Thought
s.d: the content of thinking and reasoning
s.c: In a number of languages it is simply not possible to find noun-like words for thinking or reasoning and therefore it may be necessary to use a verb equivalent throughout. For example, in ⟦Luke 11:17|Luke 11:17⟧ one may translate as ‘but Jesus knew what they were thinking.’|It may be difficult in some languages to speak of ‘taking every thought captive’ (⟦2 Corinthians 10:5|2 Corinthians 10:5⟧), but one can often say ‘to control every thought’ or ‘to make oneself think as one should.’

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations Involving Successive Generations
s.d: pertaining to someone who is born out of wedlock and is thus without legal status or rights
s.c: There may, however, be some serious problems involved in translating νόθοι in ⟦Hebrews 12:8|Hebrews 12:8⟧, especially if νόθοι must be rendered in some languages as ‘sons whose parents are not married,’ for νόθοι occurs here in a highly figurative passage speaking of God as one’s parent. It may, therefore, be necessary to employ an expression such as ‘this means you are not his real sons’ or ‘… not sons who truly belong to him.’

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Pastures and Cultivated Lands
s.d: pasture land in contrast with cultivated fields
s.c: ‘Pastures’ are often designated as ‘grass land’ or ‘cattle land.’

s.dp: Spacial Extensions › Extension From a Source
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:νομή<SDBG:νομή:000000>}[a] ‘pasture,’ {D:1.98}) extension of an area

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Suppose, Think Possible
s.d: to regard something as presumably true, but without particular certainty
s.g: to suppose; to presume; to assume; to imagine; to believe; to think
s.c: In some languages the equivalent of ‘to suppose’ or ‘to presume’ is ‘to think somewhat’ or ‘to think perhaps’ or ‘to think a little.’ In some instances the lack of certainty is spelled out clearly as ‘to think, but not with certainty’ or ‘to think, but not to know’ or ‘to think, but not to be sure.’

s.dp: Behavior and Related States › Custom, Tradition
s.d: to engage in some activity as a customary practice
s.g: to practice; to engage in; to take place customarily
s.c: This meaning is found as a variant reading only: οὗ ἐνομίζετο προσευχὴ εἶναι ‘where prayer took place’ ⟦Acts 16:13|Acts 16:13⟧ (apparatus). This expression may also be translated as ‘where people customarily prayed.’

s.dp: Communication › Law, Regulation, Ordinance
s.d: (derivative of {L:νόμος<SDBG:νόμος:000000>}[a] ‘law, rule,’ {D:33.333}) pertaining to law
s.c: It is also possible to understand νομικός in ⟦Titus 3:9|Titus 3:9⟧ as specifically the Jewish Law (see νόμος, LN 33.55).

s.dp: Communication › Law, Regulation, Ordinance
s.d: one who is an expert in interpreting religious law (with a probable exception of {S:05600301300006} (see {D:56.37}), always in reference to the Jewish Law)
s.g: interpreter of the Law; expert in the Law

s.dp: Courts and Legal Procedures › Attorney, Lawyer
s.d: a specialist in civil law
s.c: It is possible that νομικός in ⟦Titus 3:13|Titus 3:13⟧ may have designated an expert in interpreting religious law (see LN 33.338) rather than a general legal practitioner.

s.dp: True, False › Accurate, Inaccurate
s.d: pertaining to being correct according to rules and regulations

s.dp: Artifacts › Money and Monetary Units
s.d: common and official currency

s.dp: Communication › Teach
s.d: a person who is skilled in the teaching and interpretation of the law (in the NT referring to the law of the OT)
s.g: teacher of the Law; expert in the Law

s.dp: Communication › Law, Regulation, Ordinance
s.d: to give or to establish a law
s.g: to enact a law; to give a law
s.c: Though in English it is normal to speak of ‘giving a law,’ such an expression can be entirely misleading, since in some languages ‘to give a law’ can mean ‘to annul a law’ in the sense of giving back to people a rule or regulation. A more frequent expression for ‘giving a law’ may be ‘commanding a law’ or ‘ordering a law.’|In ⟦Romans 9:4|Romans 9:4⟧ νομοθεσία refers specifically to the giving of the Jewish Law.

s.dp: Communication › Law, Regulation, Ordinance
s.d: to give or to establish a law
s.g: to enact a law; to give a law
s.c: Though in English it is normal to speak of ‘giving a law,’ such an expression can be entirely misleading, since in some languages ‘to give a law’ can mean ‘to annul a law’ in the sense of giving back to people a rule or regulation. A more frequent expression for ‘giving a law’ may be ‘commanding a law’ or ‘ordering a law.’

s.dp: Communication › Law, Regulation, Ordinance
s.d: (derivative of {L:νομοθετέω<SDBG:νομοθετέω:000000>} ‘to give a law,’ {D:33.339}) one who gives or enacts laws
s.c: In a number of languages it is not possible to speak literally of a ‘lawgiver’ as ‘one who gives laws,’ for laws seem to be quite distinct from gifts. However, the same meaning is often communicated by somewhat different expressions, for example, ‘one who decides what people must do’ or ‘one who makes a law stand’ or ‘one who gives strength to a law.’

s.dp: Communication › Law, Regulation, Ordinance
s.d: a formalized rule (or set of rules) prescribing what people must do
s.c: The difference between ‘a law’ and ‘a command’ is that a law is enforced by sanctions from a society, while a command carries only the sanctions of the individual who commands. When, however, the people of Israel accepted the commands of God as the rules which they would follow and enforce, these became their laws.|The occurrence of νόμος two times in ⟦Romans 8:2|Romans 8:2⟧ poses certain problems of both translation and interpretation: ὁ γὰρ νόμος τοῦ πνεύματος τῆς ζωῆς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ ἠλευθέρωσέν σε ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμου τῆς ἁμαρτίας καὶ τοῦ θανάτου ‘for the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus freed you from the law which leads to sin and death.’ In the second occurrence of νόμος, the meaning is clearly the rules and regulations of the OT law, but in the case of the first occurrence of νόμος, there is no such formulation of decrees. The reference in this instance must therefore be to certain basic principles. If, however, one understands νόμος in the sense of a type of abstract ‘governing power,’ it is possible that the reference in the phrase νόμος τοῦ πνεύματος τῆς ζωῆς is to this governing power of the Spirit of life which frees one from the law which stipulates sin and death.

s.dp: Communication › Written Language
s.d: the first five books of the OT called the Torah (often better rendered as ‘instruction’)
s.c: In a number of languages it is not possible to use a singular expression such as ‘the Law,’ for since the Torah consisted of five books and included a number of regulations and instructions, it is necessary in many languages to use ‘the laws.’ Furthermore, to distinguish this body of laws from common, ordinary customs or legal regulations, it may be necessary to employ a phrase such as ‘the laws given to Moses’ or simply ‘the laws of Moses.’

s.dp: Communication › Written Language
s.d: the sacred writings of the OT
s.c: It is clear from the content of the quotation in ⟦John 10:34|John 10:34⟧ that the reference of νόμος is not restricted to the first five books of the OT, for the passage comes from the Psalms.

s.dp: Communication › Law, Regulation, Ordinance
s.d: (an idiom, literally: law of the man, or: law of the husband) the law which binds a woman to a man in marriage
s.c: It may be especially difficult in some languages to speak of ‘being free from the marriage law.’ An appropriate equivalent in some languages may be ‘she is no longer obliged to remain the wife of the dead man,’ but in other languages it is more meaningful to say ‘she is then permitted to marry another man.’

s.dp: Communication › Written Language
s.d: (an idiom, literally: the Law and the Prophets) all of the sacred writings of the OT, including the Law, the Prophets, and the Writings{N:001}
s.g: the sacred writings; the Law and the Prophets

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Desire, Want, Wish
s.d: to have an unhealthy or morbid desire for something
s.g: to desire in an unhealthy manner; to have a morbid desire
s.c: In some languages the closest equivalent of ‘an unhealthy desire’ would be ‘to desire something that one should not desire.’

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sickness, Disease, Weakness
s.d: the state of being diseased

s.dp: Animals › Birds
s.d: a collective for the young of birds hatched in a nest

s.dp: Animals › Birds
s.d: the young of any bird

s.dp: Animals › Birds
s.d: the young of any bird

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Steal, Rob
s.d: to misappropriate funds for one’s own benefit
s.g: to misappropriate funds for oneself; to embezzle

s.dp: Spacial Orientations › North, South, East, West
s.c: In most languages east and west are related to the rising or setting sun, although in some languages there may be some local geographical feature which serves as a marker of direction, for example, the location of a particular mountain, the ocean, or a river. For north, some languages employ ‘to the left of the rising sun,’ that is to say, the direction is oriented in terms of the left hand of a person facing toward the rising sun. Similarly, south would be ‘to the right of the rising sun.’

s.dp: Physical Events and States › Wind
s.d: a wind which blows from the south
s.c: A number of languages have terms for winds coming from or going toward different directions. In a number of cases, however, directional expressions are not included in the terms for such winds. For example, a north wind may be simply called ‘a cold wind,’ and a south wind might be called ‘a wind from the sea.’ Such expressions depend upon local geographical features. Even in the instance in which a south wind is described in terms of direction, it may be necessary to use a somewhat expanded phrase, for example, ‘a wind from the right of the rising sun.’ Such an expression is based upon the experience of a person facing the rising sun and determining the south in terms of the right side of the person.

s.dp: Communication › Teach
s.d: to provide instruction as to correct behavior and belief{N:001}
s.g: to instruct; to teach; instruction; teaching

s.dp: Communication › Warn
s.d: to advise someone concerning the dangerous consequences of some happening or action

s.dp: Communication › Teach
s.d: to provide instruction as to correct behavior and belief{N:001}
s.g: to instruct; to teach; instruction; teaching

s.dp: Communication › Rebuke
s.d: to admonish someone for having done something wrong
s.c: νουθετέω in ⟦1 Thessalonians 5:14|1 Thessalonians 5:14⟧ may also be understood in the sense of ‘to warn’ (see LN 33.424).

s.dp: Communication › Warn
s.d: to advise someone concerning the dangerous consequences of some happening or action
s.c: νουθετέω in ⟦1 Thessalonians 5:14|1 Thessalonians 5:14⟧ may also be understood in the sense of ‘to admonish’ (see LN 33.418).

s.dp: Understand › Capacity for Understanding
s.d: pertaining to ability to reason and hence understand

s.dp: Psychological Faculties
s.d: the psychological faculty of understanding, reasoning, thinking, and deciding
s.c: In some languages there is no noun such as English mind, and therefore one must use a verb expression meaning ‘to think,’ ‘to reason,’ or ‘to understand,’ depending upon the particular context. In some languages the closest equivalent of ‘mind’ may be a figurative extension of a term meaning ‘head,’ but more often than not, thinking is regarded as being in some other part of the body, for example, ‘heart’ or ‘liver.’

s.dp: Think › To Think, Thought
s.d: a particular manner or way of thinking
s.g: way of thinking; disposition; manner of thought; attitude
s.c: In a number of languages it may be necessary to render ‘way of thinking’ by a clause, for example, ‘how people think.’ In the case of ⟦1 Peter 4:1|1 Peter 4:1⟧, it may be necessary to translate ‘you too must strengthen yourselves by thinking just like Christ thought.’

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a Christian woman or man mentioned in {S:05100401500014} (text and apparatus)

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations Based upon Marriage
s.d: a woman who is about to be married or who has just been married
s.c: As in the case of ‘bridegroom’ (LN 10.56), it may be necessary in some languages to indicate with ‘bride’ whether the person has just been married or is about to be married.

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations Based upon Marriage
s.d: the wife of one’s son
s.c: For languages which do not have specific terms for ‘mother- in-law’ and ‘daughter-in-law’ it may be possible to render ⟦Luke 12:53|Luke 12:53⟧ by translating ‘women will be against the wives of their sons, and young women will be against the mothers of their husbands.’

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations Based upon Marriage
s.d: a man who is about to be married or has just been married
s.c: In a number of languages a term for bridegroom must indicate explicitly whether the marriage is about to take place or has just taken place. Therefore, one may have to employ some such phrase as ‘a man who is going to be married soon’ or ‘a man who has just been married.’ A corresponding type of expression may be required for ‘bride’ (see LN 10.57).

s.dp: Constructions › Parts and Areas of Buildings
s.d: a relatively large room, often serving as a place for a wedding
s.c: Υἱοὶ τοῦ νυμφῶνος, literally ‘sons of the wedding hall,’ is an idiom denoting the bridegroom’s friends or the wedding guests (see LN 11.7).

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: a point of time simultaneous with the event of the discourse itself

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: a time shortly before or shortly after the time of the discourse

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: a point of time simultaneous with the event of the discourse itself

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: a time shortly before or shortly after the time of the discourse

s.dp: Discourse Markers › Markers of Transition
s.d: a marker of a summary statement
s.g: and so; accordingly; meanwhile (or left untranslated)

s.dp: Time › Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
s.d: the period between sunset and sunrise

s.dp: Physical Events and States › Darkness
s.d: darkness of the night in contrast with daylight (see {D:14.40})
s.c: It is also possible to interpret νύξ in ⟦Revelation 22:5|Revelation 22:5⟧ as a period of time rather than as darkness (see LN 67.192). See also ἡμέρα LN 14.40 and its footnote.

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: (ἡμέρας τεσσεράκοντα καὶ νύκτας τεσσεράκοντα - literally, forty days and forty nights) possibly a symbolic temporal expression denoting a relatively long period of time
s.c: Most translations render ἡμέρας τεσσεράκοντα καὶ νύκτας τεσσεράκοντα as either ‘forty days and forty nights’ or ‘forty days,’ though it is possible, in view of the symbolic meaning of the number ‘forty,’ that this expression is to be understood as meaning a long period of time.

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: (expressions, literally: night and day, day and night, respectively) duration of time, either continuous or episodic, but without limits
s.g: day and night; always; constantly; continually

s.dp: Physical Impact › Pierce, Cut
s.d: to pierce with a pointed instrument; normally not as serious a wound as is implied by {L:ἐκκεντέω<SDBG:ἐκκεντέω:000000>} ‘to pierce,’ {D:19.14}

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sleep, Waking
s.d: the process of becoming sleepy
s.c: ‘To grow drowsy’ may be rendered in some languages as ‘to begin to nod’ or ‘their heads fell’ or ‘their eyes gradually closed.’|In ⟦2 Peter 2:3|2 Peter 2:3⟧ νυστάζω occurs in a highly figurative context: καὶ ἡ ἀπώλεια αὐτῶν οὐ νυστάζει, literally ‘and their destruction is not drowsy,’ meaning either ‘their destruction is imminent’ or ‘their Destroyer has been wide awake’ (see Today’s English Version).

s.dp: Time › Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
s.d: a period consisting of a night and a day (essentially similar in meaning to {L:ἡμέρα<SDBG:ἡμέρα:000000>}[a] ‘day,’ {D:67.178}, but somewhat more explicit and emphatic)

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a preacher of repentance who built an ark

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Laziness, Idleness
s.d: pertaining to being sluggish or slow to become involved in some activity

s.dp: Understand › Lack of Capacity for Understanding
s.d: (an idiom, literally: lazy as to one’s ears) to be slow to understand, with an implication of laziness

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: the back part of the body from the neck to the pelvis
s.c: The phrase τὸν νῶτον … συγκάμπτειν may be regarded as an idiom, since its meaning may be to suffer oppression and trouble. An equivalent expression for ‘and bend their backs forever’ (⟦Romans 11:10|Romans 11:10⟧) may be ‘to make them slaves forever’ or ‘to make them toil hard forever’ (see LN 24.94).

s.dp: Constructions › Parts and Areas of Buildings
s.d: a place of temporary lodging for a person away from home
s.g: guestroom; lodging for guest; place to stay in

s.dp: Association › Show Hospitality
s.d: hospitality to a stranger, that is, someone who is not regarded as a member of the extended family or a close friend
s.c: To receive a stranger as a guest is sometimes expressed idiomatically as ‘to let a stranger sit at one’s table,’ ‘to offer a bed to a stranger,’ or ‘to let a stranger enter one’s house.’|For another interpretation of ξενία in ⟦Philemon 1:22|Philemon 1:22⟧, see LN 7.31.

s.dp: Association › Show Hospitality
s.d: to receive and show hospitality to a stranger, that is, someone who is not regarded as a member of the extended family or a close friend
s.g: to show hospitality; to receive a stranger as a guest; hospitality
s.c: To receive a stranger as a guest is sometimes expressed idiomatically as ‘to let a stranger sit at one’s table,’ ‘to offer a bed to a stranger,’ or ‘to let a stranger enter one’s house.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Surprise, Astonish
s.d: (compare {L:ξένος<SDBG:ξένος:000000>} ‘unknown, surprising,’ {D:28.34}) to experience a sudden feeling of unexpected wonder
s.c: The experience of ‘surprise’ may be expressed idiomatically in some languages, for example, ‘to be left with one’s mouth open’ or ‘to have one’s eyes made wide open.’

s.dp: Association › Show Hospitality
s.d: to receive and show hospitality to a stranger, that is, someone who is not regarded as a member of the extended family or a close friend
s.g: to show hospitality; to receive a stranger as a guest; hospitality
s.c: To receive a stranger as a guest is sometimes expressed idiomatically as ‘to let a stranger sit at one’s table,’ ‘to offer a bed to a stranger,’ or ‘to let a stranger enter one’s house.’

s.dp: Know › Well Known, Clearly Shown, Revealed
s.d: pertaining to not being previously known and hence unheard of and unfamiliar

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Political
s.d: a person belonging to a socio-political group other than the reference group
s.c: Terms for ‘stranger’ or ‘foreigner’ are often based upon geographical differences or upon lack of previous knowledge. For example, ‘I was a stranger’ may be rendered as ‘I came from another country’ or ‘I was not known to any of you.’

s.dp: Association › Show Hospitality
s.d: a person who shows hospitality to guests
s.c: In rendering ‘host’ it may be necessary to employ a phrase, for example, ‘who welcomed and took care of us in his home.’

s.dp: Artifacts › Containers
s.d: (a borrowing based on Latin sextarius, a Roman measure equal to about a half liter, one pint) a kind of small pitcher or jar

s.dp: Features of Objects › Wet, Dry
s.d: to cause something to become dry
s.g: to dry out; to dry up; to wither

s.dp: Features of Objects › Wet, Dry
s.d: (derivative of {L:ξηρός<SDBG:ξηρός:000000>}[a] ‘dry,’ {D:79.80}) to become dry
s.c: It may be more appropriate in a number of languages to translate this clause in ⟦Mark 5:29|Mark 5:29⟧ as ‘and immediately her menstrual bleeding stopped.’

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Ripen, Produce Fruit, Bear Seed
s.d: (derivative of {L:ξηρός<SDBG:ξηρός:000000>}[a] ‘dry,’ {D:79.80}) to become ripe, with reference to grain which dries in the process of ripening
s.g: to become ripe; to be ripe

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sickness, Disease, Weakness
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of ξηραίνομαι[a] ‘to dry up,’ {D:79.81}) to become stiff to the point of not being able to move
s.g: to be stiff; to be paralyzed
s.c: In some languages one may express the meaning of ‘to be stiff all over’ as ‘not able to move any part of the body.’

s.dp: Features of Objects › Wet, Dry
s.d: pertaining to being dry

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sickness, Disease, Weakness
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ξηρός<SDBG:ξηρός:000000>}[a] ‘dry, withered,’ {D:79.80}) pertaining to a shrunken, withered, and hence immobile part of the body

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Land in Contrast With the Sea
s.d: dry land, in contrast with the sea
s.c: In a number of languages a clear distinction is made between terms which designate land in contrast with water and those which designate cultivated land. Even in English the normal term for land close to water is ‘shore’ or ‘coast,’ and therefore one may translate ⟦Matthew 14:24|Matthew 14:24⟧ as ‘the boat was already far away from the shore.’ Similarly, in ⟦Acts 27:27|Acts 27:27⟧ one may translate ‘we were getting close to shore.’

s.dp: Plants › Wood and Wood Products
s.d: (derivative of {L:ξύλον<SDBG:ξύλον:000000>}[a] ‘wood,’ {D:3.60}) pertaining to being made or consisting of wood

s.dp: Plants › Wood and Wood Products
s.d: wood as a substance
s.c: A number of languages make a clear distinction between wood as a substance used in artifacts and constructions and wood used for heating or cooking. A further distinction may be made between durable wood (not readily subject to rot or to the effects of termites and borers) and less durable and therefore relatively unsatisfactory wood.

s.dp: Plants › Wood and Wood Products
s.d: wood as a substance used to burn for heat
s.c: ξύλον in ⟦Luke 23:31|Luke 23:31⟧ may also be interpreted as a live green tree (see LN 3.4). If one assumes that the meaning here is ‘firewood,’ then it may be necessary to translate ‘wood which has not had an opportunity to dry out’ or ‘wood which is still green’ or ‘… which is still wet with sap.’

s.dp: Plants › Trees
s.d: large perennial plant, usually having a woody central stem, called a trunk, with secondary branches growing from it
s.c: It is also possible to understand ξύλον in ⟦Luke 23:31|Luke 23:31⟧ as ‘firewood.’ One may therefore translate the first part of this conditional sentence as ‘if they do these things to firewood which has recently been cut’ or ‘if they do these things to firewood which hasn’t dried out’ (see LN 3.61).|In ⟦Revelation 2:7|Revelation 2:7⟧ and ⟦Revelation 22:2|Revelation 22:2⟧ ξύλον τῆς ζωῆς ‘tree of life’ may cause certain complications if the passage is translated more or less literally ‘I will give him to eat of the tree of life.’ In some languages a literal rendering would mean ‘to gnaw on the tree of life,’ that is to say, to eat the wood or the bark. It may therefore be necessary to translate ‘to eat the fruit of the tree of life’ or ‘… the fruit from the tree that causes life’ or ‘… causes people to live.’

s.dp: Artifacts › Weapons and Armor
s.d: a heavy stick used in fighting

s.dp: Artifacts › Instruments Used in Binding and Fastening
s.d: an instrument consisting of heavy blocks of wood through which the legs were placed and then securely fastened
s.c: Stocks were employed primarily as an instrument for imprisonment, but also as a means of punishment.

s.dp: Artifacts › Instruments Used in Punishment and Execution
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ξύλον<SDBG:ξύλον:000000>}[a] ‘wood,’ {D:3.60}) an instrument of execution
s.c: Outside the NT ξύλον often refers to a gallows, but in the NT contexts speaking of capital punishment, the reference is to the cross on which Jesus was crucified.

s.dp: Physical Impact › Pierce, Cut
s.d: to shave the head or beard

s.dp: Discourse Referentials › Whom or What Spoken or Written About
s.d: a reference to an entity, event, or state, clearly identified by the linguistic or non-linguistic context of the utterance{N:001}

s.dp: Number › One, Two, Three, Etc. [Cardinals]
s.d: cardinal number, where there are eighty instances of a countable entity

s.dp: Number › First, Second, Third, Etc. [Ordinals]
s.d: eighth in a series involving either time, space, or set
s.c: In a number of languages one does not speak of ‘the eighth’ as being the eighth item in a set. Often it is far more usual to say ‘one together with seven others.’ This same system may apply to all ordinals in a language.

s.dp: Be, Become, Exist, Happen › Happen
s.d: that which serves to hinder or prevent someone from doing something

s.dp: Discourse Referentials › Demonstrative or Deictic Reference
s.d: a reference to an entity regarded as relatively present in terms of the discourse setting, whether preceding or following{N:001}

s.dp: Discourse Referentials › Demonstrative or Deictic Reference
s.d: a reference to indefinite alternatives
s.g: such and such; this or that

s.dp: Linear Movement › Travel, Journey
s.d: to be in the process of travelling, presumably for some distance
s.g: to travel; to be on a journey; journey

s.dp: Linear Movement › Lead, Bring, Take
s.d: to guide or to direct, with the implication of making certain that people reach an appropriate destination

s.dp: Learn
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ὁδηγέω<SDBG:ὁδηγέω:000000>}[a] ‘to lead, to guide,’ {D:15.182}) to guide someone in acquiring information{N:001}
s.g: to lead someone to know; to guide someone in learning

s.dp: Linear Movement › Lead, Bring, Take
s.d: (derivative of {L:ὁδηγέω<SDBG:ὁδηγέω:000000>}[a] ‘to guide,’ {D:15.182}) one who guides

s.dp: Guide, Discipline, Follow › Guide, Lead
s.d: one who guides or leads
s.c: In ⟦Romans 2:19|Romans 2:19⟧ the context is figurative in the sense that ‘the blind’ are those who are spiritually blind, and the guidance which they require is a proper understanding of the truth in terms of how they should behave.

s.dp: Linear Movement › Travel, Journey
s.d: to be on a journey, presumably with the focus upon being en route
s.g: to travel; to be en route; journey; trip

s.dp: Linear Movement › Travel, Journey
s.d: to be on a journey, presumably with the focus upon being en route
s.g: to travel; to be en route; journey; trip

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Thoroughfares: Roads, Streets, Paths, etc.
s.d: a general term for a thoroughfare, either within a population center or between two such centers

s.dp: Linear Movement › Travel, Journey
s.d: to be in the process of travelling, presumably for some distance
s.g: to travel; to be on a journey; journey
s.c: Note that ὁδός may also refer to a particular journey, as in ⟦Luke 2:44|Luke 2:44⟧, ἦλθον ἡμέρας ὁδόν ‘they made a day’s trip.’

s.dp: Behavior and Related States › Behavior, Conduct
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ὁδός<SDBG:ὁδός:000000>}[a] ‘road,’ {D:1.99}) a customary manner of life or behavior, with probably some implication of goal or purpose
s.g: way of life; way to live

s.dp: Behavior and Related States › Particular Patterns of Behavior
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ὁδός<SDBG:ὁδός:000000>}[a] ‘road, way,’ {D:1.99}) behavior in accordance with Christian principles and practices
s.c: In a number of languages it is impossible to preserve the figurative meaning of ὁδός in ⟦Acts 9:2|Acts 9:2⟧, and therefore it may be necessary to translate the first part of ⟦Acts 9:2|Acts 9:2⟧ simply as ‘so that if he could find any who were followers of Christ’ or ‘… those who were Christians.’

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Just, Righteous
s.d: (an idiom, literally: a straight road) the right or correct pattern of behavior
s.g: right way; correct manner of life; just way of life

s.dp: Ready, Prepared
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to prepare the road) to cause circumstances to be ready or propitious for some event
s.g: to make ready for; to prepare for; to prepare the way for
s.c: In some languages it may be better to render this expression in ⟦Matthew 11:10|Matthew 11:10⟧ as ‘who will arrange everything for you.’

s.dp: Spacial Dimensions › Specific Measures of Length
s.d: (an idiom, literally: a Sabbath’s road) a Sabbath day’s journey, somewhat over half a mile and about one kilometer
s.g: half a mile; one kilometer; Sabbath journey

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: one of a set of hard, bony structures set in the mouth of humans and many animals; used for chewing and biting
s.c: There are several problems involved in the rendering of ὀδούς. Even in the case of ⟦Revelation 9:8|Revelation 9:8⟧ it may be necessary to use two different terms for teeth, since human teeth may be referred to by expressions quite different from those used in referring to the teeth of animals. In ⟦Acts 7:54|Acts 7:54⟧ the idiom ‘to grind one’s teeth’ denotes anger (LN 88.184), but a literal rendering of ‘to grind the teeth’ may mean in some languages merely ‘to be nervous.’ The expression βρυγμὸς τῶν ὀδόντων ‘gnashing of the teeth’ is used in connection with the tortures of hell (⟦Luke 13:28|Luke 13:28⟧), but a literal rendering of such a phrase can be quite misleading, since it may refer merely to the eating of some hard substance. See LN 23.41.
